about: Curated region reference for the Fly Atlas. Families follow the standard supercategories of Ito et al. (2014) Neuron 81:755 (brain) and Court et al. (2020) Neuron 108:1 (nerve cord), as used by FlyWire. Functions are kept to what is well established; where little is known, the text says so.

families.name: Optic lobe
families.desc: The two big visual centres behind the eyes. Signals from the photoreceptors pass layer by layer through the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate, which pull out contrast, colour, motion and object features before sending them on to the central brain.

families.name: Mushroom body
families.desc: The fly's learning centre. Kenyon cells receive smell (and some visual and taste) information in the calyx and send long axons through the pedunculus into the lobes. There, dopamine neurons signal reward or punishment and output neurons read out the learned value.

families.name: Central complex
families.desc: A chain of midline structures that keep track of which way the fly is facing and help it steer toward goals. It holds the fly's internal compass.

families.name: Lateral complex
families.desc: Paired regions next to the central complex. The bulb feeds visual cues into the compass, the gall links to compass neurons, and the lateral accessory lobe sends steering signals to descending neurons.

families.name: Superior neuropils
families.desc: The top of the central brain, where smell, taste and other senses are combined with hunger, thirst and learned value. Many mushroom-body output and dopamine neurons connect here.

families.name: Inferior neuropils
families.desc: Regions around the mushroom-body lobes and the midline. They are heavily wired but their jobs are still poorly understood.

families.name: Ventrolateral neuropils
families.desc: The sides of the central brain, where visual projection neurons from the optic lobe and hearing/wind neurons from the antenna arrive and are processed into features like looming objects or courtship song.

families.name: Ventromedial neuropils
families.desc: The lower middle of the central brain. Many descending neurons, which carry commands to the nerve cord, pick up their inputs here, including visual motion signals used for flight and head control.

families.name: Periesophageal neuropils
families.desc: The regions wrapped around the oesophagus: hearing, wind and gravity sensing from the antenna, and feeding- and hormone-related neurons.

families.name: Ventral nerve cord
families.desc: The fly's equivalent of a spinal cord, in the thorax. It holds the motor circuits for walking and flight and receives touch and position sense from the body. In the BANC and male CNS scans it is wired to the brain.

families.name: Not a brain region
families.desc: Synapses that sit in peripheral nerves or could not be assigned to any named region.

LA.desc: The first layer behind the eye. Each of about 800 'cartridges' collects input from the R1–6 photoreceptors that look at one point in space and passes it to lamina neurons L1–L5.

ME.desc: The largest visual region, built of about 800 columns and ten layers. Colour photoreceptors R7 and R8 end here, and its circuits start computing contrast, colour and the direction of motion.

AME.desc: A small region at the front edge of the medulla. Clock neurons that make the neuropeptide PDF branch here and receive light information that helps reset the daily clock. The clock itself is a network of about 240 neurons spread across the brain (the count from the FlyWire connectome; older textbooks say about 150).

LO.desc: A deeper visual region that detects features such as small moving objects and looming. Its lobula columnar (LC) neurons carry these features to glomeruli in the central brain.

LOP.desc: Receives direction-selective motion signals from T4 and T5 cells, one layer per direction. Large tangential cells here sense whole-field motion (optic flow) used to keep the fly on course.

AL.desc: The first smell centre, with about 50 glomeruli. Each glomerulus collects the smell neurons that carry one type of odour receptor; projection neurons then carry the signal to the mushroom body and lateral horn.

LH.desc: Receives smell information from the antennal lobe and drives built-in (unlearned) reactions, such as attraction to food odours or avoidance of danger smells.

MB_CA.desc: Where projection neurons carrying smell (and some visual and taste) information connect to the Kenyon cells of the mushroom body.

MB_PED.desc: The stalk of Kenyon cell axons running from the calyx to the lobes.

MB_VL.desc: One of the output lobes. Dopamine neurons here signal reward or punishment, changing how Kenyon cells talk to mushroom-body output neurons.

MB_ML.desc: The other output lobe, organised like the vertical lobe into compartments, each with its own dopamine and output neurons.

EB.desc: A ring-shaped structure where E-PG neurons keep a 'bump' of activity that tracks the fly's heading, like an internal compass. Ring neurons bring in visual landmarks.

PB.desc: A bar-shaped structure where the heading signal from the ellipsoid body is laid out left-to-right and passed to other central-complex neurons.

FB.desc: The largest central-complex structure. It combines heading with travel direction and goals to guide steering, and some of its layers help control sleep.

NO.desc: Small paired structures under the fan-shaped body that bring self-motion (speed and turning) signals into the central complex.

AB.desc: A small structure near the fan-shaped body, usually larger on one side. It has been linked to long-term memory, but its role is not well understood.

LAL.desc: Receives central-complex output and connects to descending neurons that turn the fly while walking or flying.

BU.desc: Relays visual information such as landmarks, the sun and polarised light from the anterior optic tubercle to the ring neurons of the ellipsoid body.

GA.desc: A small region where certain ellipsoid-body/protocerebral-bridge columnar neurons connect; part of the navigation loop.

SLP.desc: Next to the lateral horn. Receives smell information and links it with signals about the body's nutritional state.

SIP.desc: A zone where mushroom-body output neurons and dopamine neurons connect, linking learned value to behaviour.

SMP.desc: A large midline region that integrates hunger, thirst and other internal states with learned and sensory information; many neurosecretory and mushroom-body-related neurons connect here.

CRE.desc: Wraps the mushroom-body lobes and holds many mushroom-body output and dopamine neuron branches.

SCL.desc: A densely wired region that clamps around the mushroom-body pedunculus. Its specific role is still poorly understood.

ICL.desc: Lies below the superior clamp. It receives visual projections among other inputs, but its role is still poorly understood.

IB.desc: A midline region joining the two hemispheres. Its function is still poorly understood.

ATL.desc: A small region next to the inferior bridge. Its function is still poorly understood. (It is not part of the central complex.)

AOTU.desc: Receives visual features such as colour and polarised light from the optic lobe and passes them on, via the bulb, toward the central-complex compass.

AVLP.desc: A large region processing auditory information (including courtship song) and visual features.

PVLP.desc: Where many lobula columnar neurons end in glomeruli, each signalling a visual feature such as a looming object.

PLP.desc: Another major target of visual projection neurons from the optic lobe.

WED.desc: Secondary processing of hearing and wind signals coming from the antenna (Johnston's organ).

VES.desc: A ventromedial region where many descending neurons collect input; its exact roles are still being mapped.

EPA.desc: A small ventromedial region near the vest. Its function is still poorly understood.

GOR.desc: A small ventromedial region near the vest and epaulette. Its function is still poorly understood.

SPS.desc: Receives visual motion information (for example from lobula-plate tangential cells) and passes it to descending neurons for flight and head control.

IPS.desc: Like the superior posterior slope, links visual motion and other signals to descending neurons.

SAD.desc: Surrounds the AMMC and processes mechanosensory signals from the antenna's Johnston's organ: sound, wind and gravity.

AMMC.desc: Where Johnston's organ neurons in the antenna deliver sound, wind and gravity information; it also contains antenna motor neurons.

FLA.desc: A region where neurosecretory (hormone-releasing) neurons of the pars intercerebralis and feeding-related neurons project. It also holds many sex-specific (doublesex) neurons.

CAN.desc: A small region near the flange. Its function is still poorly understood.

PRW.desc: The midline region that receives taste input from the pharynx and contains feeding-related neurons.

GNG.desc: Receives taste input from the mouthparts and legs, contains motor neurons for feeding, and is a major source and target of descending neurons.

ProNm.desc: Holds the walking circuits and motor neurons for the front legs and receives their touch and position sense.

MesoNm.desc: Holds the walking circuits and motor neurons for the middle legs.

MetaNm.desc: Holds the walking circuits and motor neurons for the hind legs.

ANm.desc: Controls the abdomen, including mating, egg-laying and gut-related functions.

NTct.desc: Part of the dorsal 'tectulum' that controls the neck muscles and head movement.

WTct.desc: Contains the flight motor circuits and wing motor neurons.

HTct.desc: Receives input from and controls the halteres, the small knobbed organs that act as gyroscopes during flight.

IntTct.desc: A band of neuropil between the dorsal flight regions and the leg neuromeres. Its function is only partly understood.

LTct.desc: The lower part of the tectulum, thought to help coordinate legs and wings; its function is only partly understood.

AMNp.desc: A dense region where the front and middle segments of the cord meet. It mostly receives sensory nerves from the wing and the notum (the back of the thorax). The male CNS scan calls it the ovoid (Ov); it is the same region.

mVAC.desc: Receives the endings of chordotonal sensory neurons in the legs, which sense vibration and leg position; it resembles the 'auditory' neuropil of other insects.

nerves.desc: Synapses found inside the nerves that enter and leave the nerve cord, outside any neuropil.

unassigned.desc: Synapses the scan could not assign to a named region. In Maxime's scan most of these were labelled only as 'tectulum' without saying which part.

maxime.MB_ML: Maxime's export assigns very few synapses to the mushroom-body lobes compared with the calyx; this is probably how the BANC export labels these regions, not biology.
